description: Temelleri Bahçeşehir Üniversitesi Yapay Zeka Mühendisliği öğrencileri tarafından atılan AI Gambit, adını satrançtaki stratejik ve öncü hamlelerden alan bir teknoloji takımıdır. Odak noktamız; yapay zeka, makine öğrenmesi ve veri bilimi teknolojilerini kullanarak gerçek dünya problemlerine ölçeklenebilir ve akıllı çözümler üretmektir. Akademik bilgimizi hızlı prototipleme yeteneğimizle birleştirerek yenilikçi projeler geliştiriyor, ulusal ve uluslararası teknoloji yarışmalarında yer alıyoruz.
summary:
Team AI Gambit built an offline health-monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions, running on three computers on a single local network with no link to Earth required.

On the ship, each crew member sees their own readings, status, self-care tasks and a daily check-in, and can ask a built-in assistant questions in plain language. The Earth-side station is a read-only crew view that receives privacy-filtered data: mood and stress reach the ground only if the astronaut chooses to share them. A third machine runs the language model locally.

Our core design rule is that numbers always come from the data, never from the model. Every value and alert is produced by a deterministic rule engine whose thresholds trace to NASA-STD-3001 and published spaceflight studies; the assistant only explains them, and alerts keep working if the model is unavailable.

We demonstrate the system on a mission dataset built from real NASA OSDR data, ISS DOSTEL-2 radiation telemetry and Inspiration4 crew serum panels, extended with simulated days for 180-day ISS and 860-day Mars scenarios.

This matters because crews beyond low Earth orbit face communication delays that rule out real-time medical support from the ground.
details: Our project is an offline health-monitoring system for astronauts on long missions such as a Mars transit, where a 20+ minute communication delay means the crew cannot wait for Earth to answer. It runs on three computers on a local network with no internet or cloud. On the ship station, each astronaut logs in to see their daily readings: cardiovascular, sleep, bone, immune, behavioural and cabin exposure, compared with healthy ranges. They also get a clear status, self-care actions and a short daily check-in. An onboard assistant answers questions about their own data, with source badges that show where each number comes from. If the assistant can't reach its main service, it falls back to a local language model and then to an offline rule-based answer. The Earth base station receives a privacy-filtered downlink and shows mission control a read-only overview of the crew. The benefit is earlier detection of health problems and more crew autonomy when real-time medical support is impossible. The intended impact is to show how AI can support crew health safely in deep space. We built it with Python (FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite), React and TypeScript (Vite, Tailwind, Recharts), and Qwen 2.5 running locally through Ollama on ordinary laptops. What makes it creative is the safety design around the AI: the language model never produces numbers, every number in an answer is checked against the data, and alerts and emergency-symptom detection are rule-based, so they keep working even when the AI is off. Our team also considered privacy and crew autonomy, so mood and stress data reach Earth only when the astronaut chooses to share them. We also designed for communication delay, offline operation on limited hardware, a bilingual Turkish/English interface, and accessibility: status is always shown with icons and text, never colour alone.
